method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-02.
questions: A numerical pattern needs an account of how the cases and measurements were produced. A change after an intervention does not by itself establish the intervention's effect. A dramatic result can reflect selective reporting, extreme-case selection, or a search through many possibilities. Different errors require different repairs: better comparisons, clearer denominators, or new evidence. Statistics becomes useful when the design supports the inference being made.

used_for: Compare with what would otherwise happen
Discovery and confirmation need different work

evidence.excerpt: This fallacy occurs during causal reasoning when a causal connection between two kinds of events is claimed when evidence is available indicating that both are the effect of a common cause.
Suppose we notice that an event of kind A is followed in time by an event of kind B, and then hastily leap to the conclusion that A caused B.
This is the mistake of over-emphasizing the strength of a piece of evidence while paying insufficient attention to the context.
Suppose that pool has six million people who could have committed the crime, all other things being equal.
This fallacy occurs when regression to the mean is mistaken for a sign of a causal connection.
There is most probably nothing causing people from Dayton to be more like the average resident of the U.S.; but rather what is happening is that averages are regressing to the mean.
The Sharpshooter’s Fallacy gets its name from someone shooting a rifle at the side of the barn and then going over and drawing a target and bulls eye concentrically around the bullet hole.
Intentionally failing to use information suspected of being relevant and significant is committing the fallacy of suppressed evidence.

If the relevant information is not intentionally suppressed but rather inadvertently overlooked, the fallacy of suppressed evidence also is said to occur, although the fallacy’s name is misleading in this case.

sources.annotation: Secondary explanations of specific argument errors, with context-sensitive distinctions and legitimate alternatives; no universal verdict is inferred from a label.
